title: Wanderers: How Planets Move Across the Sky
objective: After this level you can explain why planets drift against the stars and sometimes appear to loop backwards.
summary: Planets drift against the stars as they orbit. When Earth overtakes an outer planet, it seems to go backwards: retrograde motion.

cards.headline: Every few years, Mars seems to stop, reverse and loop back across the sky.
cards.body: It never actually turns around. You're watching from a moving planet, and that changes what you see.

cards.headline: The wanderers
cards.body: Night after night, the stars hold their patterns. Planets don't: they slowly shift position against the background stars as they orbit the Sun, always keeping to the ecliptic road from Level 15. The ancient Greeks noticed these drifting lights, and the word "planet" comes from their word for "wanderer." The stars stay put; the planets go for a stroll.

cards.headline: Overtaking on the inside lane
cards.body: Earth orbits closer to the Sun than Mars does, and it moves faster. Every so often Earth, on its faster inner orbit, catches up with Mars and overtakes it. For a while, Mars appears to slide backwards against the stars, then it carries on forward. You've seen this on the highway: pass a slower car and it seems to drift backwards, though you're both going forward.

cards.context: No planet ever reverses direction in its orbit. The backwards loop is a change in our viewpoint, not in the planet's path. Mars has no idea it's doing anything strange.

mascot.line: Hold on to this overtaking trick. In Level 24 it helps knock Earth out of the center.

cards.headline: Wanderers: explained
learned: Planets drift against the stars as they orbit
Earth overtaking Mars makes it seem to go backwards

questions.prompt: What does the word “planet” originally mean?

options.label: Round world
options.rationale: The name comes from how planets move, not their shape.

options.label: Bright star
options.rationale: Planets were named for moving against the stars.

questions.explanation: Planets drift against the fixed patterns of stars, so the Greeks called them “wanderers.”

questions.prompt: Why does Mars sometimes appear to move backwards across the sky?

options.label: Mars reverses its orbit for a few weeks
options.rationale: Planets never reverse; this is an illusion.

options.label: The Sun pulls Mars backwards
options.rationale: The Sun’s gravity doesn’t make Mars reverse.

options.label: Mars is hidden behind the Moon
options.rationale: That would hide Mars, not move it.

options.label: Earth, on its faster inner orbit, is overtaking it

questions.explanation: Earth moves faster than Mars. As Earth passes Mars, Mars appears to slip backwards against the stars, just like a slower car you overtake.

questions.prompt: From Level 3: which of these planets can show retrograde motion caused by Earth overtaking it?

options.label: Mercury
options.rationale: Mercury orbits inside Earth’s orbit, so Earth never overtakes it.

options.label: Venus
options.rationale: Venus orbits inside Earth’s orbit and moves faster than Earth.

options.label: Earth
options.rationale: We watch from Earth; it can’t appear to move against the stars.

questions.explanation: Mars is the rocky planet just outside Earth’s orbit. Earth overtakes it every couple of years, causing its retrograde loop.
